questions.question: I remember something better if I write it down.
My written work doesn’t look neat to me. My papers have crossed-out words and erasures.
I get lost or am late if someone tells me how to get to a new place, and I don’t write down the directions.
I tend to solve problems through a more trial-and-error approach, rather than from a step-by-step method.
I am not skilled in giving verbal explanations or directions.
I understand how to do something if someone tells me, rather than having to read the same thing to myself.
It’s hard for me to understand a joke when someone tells me.
I learn best when I am shown how to do something, and I have the opportunity to do it.
When I can’t think of a specific word, I’ll use my hands a lot and call something a “what-cha-ma-call-it” or a “thing-a-ma-jig.”
I remember things that I hear, rather than things that I see or read.
It is better for me to get work done in a quiet place.
I enjoy doodling and even my notes have lots of pictures and arrows in them.
It helps to use my finger as a pointer when reading to keep my place.
I think better when I have the freedom to move around.
It’s hard for me to read other people’s handwriting.
Papers with very small print, blotchy dittos or poor copies are tough on me.
Using flashcards helps me to retain material for tests.
I don’t like to read directions; I’d rather just start doing.
I do not become easily lost, even in strange surroundings.
If I am taking a test, I can “see” the textbook page and where the answer is located.
Before I follow directions, it helps me to see someone else do it first.
If I had the choice to learn new information through a lecture or textbook, I would choose to hear it rather than read it.
Studying at a desk is not for me.
My eyes get tired fast, even though the eye doctor says that my eyes are ok.
When I read, I mix up words that look alike, such as “them” and “then,” “bad” and “dad.”
I find myself needing frequent breaks while studying.
It helps me to look at the person while listening; it keeps me focused.
When trying to remember someone’s telephone number, or something new like that, it helps me to get a picture of it in my mind.
It’s hard for me to understand what a person is saying when there are people talking or music playing.
Writing is tiring. I press down too hard with my pen or pencil.
I enjoy challenging myself by setting personal goals that help me grow in mathematics.

I find it satisfying to use different strategies and tools (e.g. creating study plan, applying real-world contexts, using digital apps, using artificial intelligence) that help me understand mathematics better.
I enjoy practicing mathematics problems because it helps me improve my skills.
I am curious about mathematics and enjoy exploring different problem-solving methods.
When I face difficulties in mathematics, I stay motivated and keep trying until I understand.
I view challenging mathematics problems as opportunities to learn and grow.
I feel fulfilled when I make progress in mathematics because I genuinely enjoy learning and improving.
I can manage learning mathematics with minimal assistance from my teacher.
If I struggle with a mathematics problem, I can find different strategies to solve it.
I am confident that I can handle unexpected challenges in mathematics.
I feel certain that I can grasp complex mathematics problems after working through them.
I have a designated space specifically for studying mathematics that is free from distractions.
Feelings of fatigue or burnout often interfere with my ability to study mathematics effectively.
I frequently use techniques such as summarization, problem-solving practice, and diagramming while studying mathematics.
I review my mathematics notes regularly after classes.
I manage my study time effectively when preparing for mathematics assignments and examination.
I create a study schedule specifically for mathematics and stick to it.
I am satisfied with my current mathematics study habits.
My study habits contribute to my success in mathematics.
The classroom environment makes me feel comfortable asking questions when I don’t understand something in mathematics.
The pace at which my mathematics teacher presents new material allows me to fully grasp each topic before moving on.
The feedback I receive from my mathematics teacher helps me understand my mistakes and improve my skills.
Working in groups or participating in collaborative activities helps me better understand and learn mathematical concepts.
The way mathematics is taught in my class makes me more interested in the subject.
My mathematics teacher provides individual attention when extra help is needed.
The use of technology (e.g., calculators, computers, online resources) in my mathematics class helps me understand the material better.
